title: Nikola Tesla's Life In Reverse | From a New York Hotel to a Storm Village
description:
Nikola Tesla's life runs backwards in this episode, opening with his death in a Manhattan hotel room in 1943 and rewinding to his birth in the frontier village of Smiljan in 1856. The journey steps through the Long Island transmitter station he never finished, the Colorado Springs lightning yard, the radio controlled boat of 1898, the motor patents sold to Westinghouse and the Budapest telephone exchange where he first earned wages. Every scene moves to an earlier year, so the alternating current system arrives in reverse order and its costs become clear. Dates, patents and places follow the documented record, and his later claims are reported as claims.

scenes.narration: Today an SI unit of magnetic flux density is named the tesla, a name agreed by physicists in 1960. His ashes sit in a gold sphere in a museum in Belgrade, and a museum also stands in the village where he was born. Statues of him look out over city squares, and almost every power grid on earth runs on his patents.

Eighty-three years before that, on January 7, 1943, Nikola Tesla was found dead in room 3327 of the New Yorker Hotel in Manhattan. He was eighty-six years old. The official cause was a heart condition. He was cremated in New York, and the box of ashes was sent to Yugoslavia at the request of his home country.

Within days of his death, agents of the American government entered the hotel rooms and seized his papers, his crates of instruments and his correspondence. The material was examined in the weeks that followed. Some of it was returned to relatives and visitors, and the rest entered government files, where researchers have studied it ever since.

Two months later, in March 1943, the highest American court ruled on a patent case he had brought against Guglielmo Marconi in 1915. The court upheld Tesla's radio patents. He had lost control of them decades earlier and never collected a fee, and the decision arrived after his death, when he could no longer read it.

Through the last twenty years of his life he moved between Manhattan hotels, ran up bills he could not pay, and fed the pigeons in the city parks every afternoon. He kept working on papers and plans in his room, but the laboratories were gone. He had once had six assistants and a floor of instruments, and now he had a window.

In 1934 he gave a newspaper interview in which he said he had designed a beam weapon that could bring down aircraft at long range and stop armies at a border. He called it a new instrument of defence. No working device was ever demonstrated, and the claim belongs to the record of what he said rather than what he built.

Three years before that, in July 1931, he appeared on the cover of Time magazine at the age of seventy-five, as the press was still interested in his energy and his forecasts. Reporters asked him about wireless power, about machines that would think, and about travel at great speed. He answered them in detail, and he was rarely short of plans.

Fifteen years before that, in 1928, he filed a patent for an aircraft that would lift off vertically and then fly on tandem rotors. The drawings show a machine with its engines set in the body and its wings folded for takeoff. He never built it. The patent office recorded the design, and the machine stayed on paper.

Twenty-six years before that, in 1917, the tower at Wardenclyffe on Long Island was pulled down and the land was sold to cover debts. He had intended it as a station that would send messages and power across the ocean. The steel went for scrap, the laboratory roof stayed on for years afterwards, and the dream of global transmission ended on the site.

Two years before that, in 1915, he had sued the Marconi company over its claim to have invented radio. The case dragged through the courts for years and he won no money from it during his lifetime. He was short of cash in the period, and he wrote to his lawyer in the same weeks that he sold personal property.

In 1913 and 1914 he took out patents on a bladeless turbine, a flat disc design that spun steam or gas between smooth discs instead of catching it on vanes. He believed it would replace the heavy machinery of power stations. A few were built and tested in the years that followed, but the design never took the market.

Eleven years before that, in 1904, his financier stopped paying. The money that had built the transmitter station on Long Island dried up, and the workmen stood down. He sold shares, moved offices and wrote letters that went unanswered. Within a decade he had given up the land, and he spent the rest of his life without a laboratory of his own.

In 1901 he had begun building that station at Shoreham on Long Island, with a wooden tower a hundred and eighty feet high designed by an architect of the New York firm that had built Grand Central. He had raised a large sum from a New York banker for a share of the enterprise. Everything was laid out for transatlantic transmission.

Three years earlier, between May 1899 and January 1900, he had worked at Colorado Springs, where he built a generating station and produced artificial lightning from a mast on the prairie. His notes describe discharges visible for miles and tests of how electrical energy moves through the ground. He also wrote down rhythmic signals which he thought might come from another planet.

In October 1898 he demonstrated a small boat controlled by radio at an electrical exhibition in Madison Square Garden in New York. The crowd watched it turn and stop on command and assumed trickery, and he had to explain that no one was aboard. He patented the radio control system that same year, and it became the basis of remote steering.

Two years after that, in 1896, the power station at Niagara Falls began sending electricity to Buffalo, New York, using the polyphase system built on his patents. The current changed direction many times a second on the way. The scheme that engineers had argued about for a decade worked, and it settled how cities would receive their power.

In 1893 his system lit the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where the fairgrounds glowed at night for millions of visitors. The same year he and his rival gave public lectures on electrical light, and the two men sat on the same stage while their systems were compared. The fair showed that alternating current could be handled safely in public.

In 1891 he introduced the coil that carried his name, a transformer that raised voltage to very high frequencies and threw sparks into the air from a closed room. He demonstrated it to an engineering society in New York, then in London and Paris the following year. Wireless lighting of sealed tubes followed, and other physicists began studying the effects.

Three years earlier, in 1888, he sold and licensed his motor patents to the Westinghouse company for cash and shares, on terms that paid him a fee for each horsepower sold. The motor used a rotating magnetic field instead of mechanical switching. The arrangement made him a figure in the industry and gave American factories their standard drive.

A year before that, in 1887, he had rented a workshop on South Fifth Avenue in Manhattan and set up instruments, batteries and models of his motor. He worked with a couple of assistants and tested designs day after day. By the spring of 1888 he had a working model ready to show to engineers.

Three years before that, in 1884, he had arrived in New York from Europe with a small amount of money and a letter of introduction from a Paris employer to a man who ran the American electric light company. He worked there for about a year on dynamos, improving their performance, then left to build his own motor and his own company.

Before that he had spent two years in Paris, from 1882 to 1884, installing electric lighting for the company that had employed him in Europe. He walked the streets of the city, kept careful accounts, and worked on the design of an induction motor in the evenings. He was twenty-six, and the design was already close.

In 1882, in a park in Budapest, he said he saw the whole arrangement of a rotating magnetic field in a flash while walking with a friend, and recited poetry to explain it. He sketched it in the sand and in a notebook afterwards. The idea was the heart of the motor he would sell six years later.

A year earlier, in 1881, he had helped to fit out the telephone exchange in Budapest, tracking faults and keeping the boards running for a city that was just getting connected. He had left his studies to take the job. The work taught him how a young network fails, and he began redesigning the equipment in his head.

Two years earlier, in the autumn of 1880, he had gone to Prague to sit in on classes he had missed, studying physics and mathematics at the university there. He arrived without the full preparation that other students had, and he left without a degree. He read on his own and kept notes on machines that no one had asked him to build.

From 1875 he had studied electrical engineering at the technical college in Graz on a military scholarship. He was good with arithmetic and quick with machines, and he built devices in the workshops. He sat no final examination, and he left after five years without completing his degree, and the loss of the diploma stayed with him for the rest of his life.

In 1873, at the age of seventeen, he fell seriously ill with cholera and was bedridden for months in the family house. He recovered, and the illness changed the direction of his schooling, because he was then allowed to go to the technical school he had asked his father to let him attend.

From 1870 to 1873 he had attended the higher real school in Karlovac, walking and riding to the town each day. The classes were taught in German, and the curriculum was practical rather than classical, with drawing, physics and mechanics on the timetable. His father, a priest, wanted him to follow him into the church.

His father was a Serbian Orthodox priest and his mother came from a farming family in the same region. The village of Smiljan sat in a military frontier district of the Austrian empire, and the household was modest. His mother, who could not read, made household tools herself, and later in life he credited her memory and her hands.

He was born on July 10, 1856, in Smiljan, in what is now Croatia, the son of Milutin Tesla, a priest, and Juka Mandic. Family tradition says that he came early during a violent thunderstorm, and his mother always connected his arrival with the weather. He was the fourth of the children, and he grew up among fields, churches and frontier roads.
